newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gold mine job cuts worry S.African labour minister.
newsitem.headline: Gold mine job cuts worry S.African labour minister.

text.p: South Africa's Minister of Labour Tito Mboweni said on Wednesday that job cuts in the mining industry were worrying and urged management not to make extreme decisions based on a mine's single bad performance.

"There are complex structures involved and some very marginal mines, but we are very concerned given the country's overall unemployment situation. Job losses in mining and other sectors is really not helping," Mboweni told Reuters.
Mboweni was commenting on mining house JCI Ltd's announcement earlier on Wednesday that it planned to cut between 3,400 and 4,100 jobs on May 31 at its Randfontein Estates Gold Mining Co Ltd.
"The recent retrenchment plans at Randfontein and other mines is not an encouraging picture at all," he said.
South African gold mines are severely pressured due to falling output, rising costs and a sickly bullion price.
The March quarter gold results were disappointing overall and under such circumstances jobs are the first things to be targeted by cost-cutting measures.

Randfontein produced 4,392 kg of gold in the March quarter compared to 5,100 kg in the December quarter. It plunged into a loss of 2.86 million rand compared with the previous quarter's 43.83 million rand profit.

"With all fairness, JCI came to brief us about the situation. We advised them to discuss it with the unions concerned. Perhaps they shouldn't make such drastic decisions on the basis of one poor quarter," Mboweni said.
But analysts said that retrenchments were the only way JCI could ensure the survival of Randfontein and the situation was much the same for other marginal mines.
Mines statistics show that the number of workers employed on gold mines has fallen sharply to 342,439 by the end of 1996 from 505,262 in 1986.

"Generally there seems to be a trend towards the reduction of jobs in the mining industry which is a cause for concern because mining has traditionally been one of the largest employers in the country," Mboweni said.
He urged mine management to commit to repositioning and retraining retrenched employees wherever possible so as to limit the social and economic impacts of job cuts.
